solution.description: Begin at the rightmost column: multiply the units digit of 1234, which is 4, by the units digit of 123, which is 3. The product 12 is two digits, so write 2 as the units digit of the answer and carry 1 into the next column.

Move one column left and cross-multiply: the tens digit 3 times the units digit 3, plus the units digit 4 times the tens digit 2, giving 17. Add the 1 carried from the previous column to get 18, so write 8 in the tens place and carry 1.

Widen the cross to three pairs now that all three digits of 123 are in play: hundreds 2 times units 3, tens 3 times tens 2, and units 4 times hundreds 1, which total 16. Adding the carried 1 gives 17, so write 7 in the hundreds place and carry 1.

Slide the same three-way cross one column further left: thousands 1 times units 3, hundreds 2 times tens 2, and tens 3 times hundreds 1, totalling 10. With the carried 1 this becomes 11, so write 1 in the thousands place and carry 1.
Only two pairs still overlap: thousands 1 times tens 2, and hundreds 2 times hundreds 1, which total 4. Adding the carried 1 gives 5, written in the ten thousands place with nothing left to carry.

solution.operation: Multiply the leftmost digits (thousands by hundreds)
solution.description: Finish with the leftmost vertical product, the thousands digit 1 of 1234 times the hundreds digit 1 of 123, which is 1, and no carry remains to add to it. Reading the digits collected from left to right gives 151782.

Write the tens digit 3 first; when multiplying a two-digit number by 11 the leading digit is carried straight into the answer.
Insert the sum of the two digits, 3 plus 2 equals 5, between them. The sum is below 10, so it sits in the middle place untouched.
Write the units digit 2 unchanged as the final digit of the product.
Read the three parts in order, 3 then 5 then 2, to get the product 352.

Write the tens digit 9 first as the provisional leading digit of the answer.
Add the two digits: 9 plus 3 is 12. This sum is two digits, so only the 2 can stay in the middle place and the 1 has to move left.
Carry that 1 into the leading digit: 9 plus 1 is 10, so the front of the answer becomes 10 rather than 9.
The units digit 3 is untouched by the carry and stays as the last digit of the product.
Assemble the settled parts, 10 then the reduced middle digit 2 then 3, which reads as 1023.

Add the carried 1 to the leading digit: 8 plus 1 is 9, which corrects the front of the answer.
The units digit 7 is unaffected by the carry and remains the last digit of the product.
Assemble the settled parts, 9 then 5 then 7, giving the product 957.

examples.problem_statement: Imagine that Able Baker Charlie has an order for 15 dozen donuts. How many donuts does he need to bake?

solution.description: Convert dozens to individual units by multiplying by 12
Set up the multiplication using Vedic Math method
Write down 0, carry over 1
Multiply crosswise and add the carried over 1
The leftmost vertical product, 1 times 1, is 1 and fills the hundreds place of the answer.
Final answer: 15 dozen = 180 donuts
Lay out the shortcut for multiplying by 12: keep the leading digit 2, then for each digit that follows, double the digit to its left and add the digit itself, working left to right.
Evaluate the chain in order: the leading 2, then (2 times 2) plus 3 equals 7, then (3 times 2) plus 4 equals 10, then the final 4 doubled with nothing to its right gives 8, producing 2 / 7 / 10 / 8.
Settle the carry: the 10 in the third slot leaves 0 and passes 1 to the 7, making it 8, so the chain 2 / 7 / 10 / 8 collapses to 2808.

Build the same chain for 2456: the leading 2, then (2 times 2) plus 4 equals 8, (4 times 2) plus 5 equals 13, (5 times 2) plus 6 equals 16, and finally 6 doubled equals 12, giving 2 / 8 / 13 / 16 / 12.
Work the carries from the right: the 12 leaves 2 and passes 1 into 16, which becomes 17, so the chain now reads 2 / 8 / 13 / 17 / 2.
Continue carrying leftward: 17 leaves 7 and passes 1 into 13, making 14; that 14 leaves 4 and passes 1 into 8, making 9. The settled chain 2 / 9 / 4 / 7 / 2 reads as 29472.

solution.description: We are dividing 26 by 9 using the Vedic sutra 'Nikhilam Navatashcaramam' (All from 9, Last from 10), which simplifies division by 9.

solution.operation: Write the dividend as digits separated by a vertical bar
solution.description: In the Vedic method, we split the two-digit number into its tens digit (2) and units digit (6). The tens digit becomes the initial quotient.
For division by 9, the first digit of the dividend (left of the bar) is the quotient, provided the sum of the digits is less than 9.

solution.operation: Compute the remainder by adding the digits
solution.description: The sutra gives the remainder as the sum of the dividend's digits, so adding the tens digit 2 and the units digit 6 gives a remainder of 8.

solution.operation: Check if remainder is less than divisor
solution.description: Since the remainder (8) is less than the divisor (9), no carry-over or adjustment is needed. The quotient and remainder are final.
Multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder should equal the original dividend. This confirms the answer is correct.
Split 53 at the units place into 5 and 3, so the tens digit stands alone on the left ready to serve as the quotient.
The part left of the split, 5, is the quotient, because each ten contains one nine with one left over.
Add the two digits to get the remainder, 5 plus 3 equals 8. Since 8 is still smaller than the divisor 9, the quotient 5 and remainder 8 are final.
Split 132 at the units place into 13 and 2, taking 13 as the starting value for the quotient.
Correct that starting value by adding the leading digit 1, giving 13 plus 1 equals 14. The extra 1 accounts for the nine hidden inside the hundreds place, so the quotient is 14.
Add every digit of the dividend for the remainder, 1 plus 3 plus 2 equals 6. As 6 is less than 9, no further adjustment is needed and the division is complete.

common_mistakes: Treating a digit sum of 9 or more as the final remainder; another nine divides out, so the quotient must go up by one.
Using only the last two digits for the remainder of a three-digit dividend; 132 needs 1 plus 3 plus 2, not 3 plus 2.
